overview: Northern Liang was a regional kingdom along the Hexi Corridor of northwestern China, established in 397 and later ruled by the Juqu family. Its position connected important routes between China and Central Asia. The atlas displays a Gansu outline from about 400 to 500, but the kingdom there ended in 439. A later Juqu continuation around Gaochang lay farther west, outside this polygon.

periods.title: Duan Ye and the first regime
periods.summary: A rebellion established Duan Ye as ruler before Juqu Mengxun took power.

periods.title: Juqu rule in the Hexi Corridor
periods.summary: Juqu Mengxun and his successors presided over a regional center of scholarship and Buddhist patronage.

periods.title: Conquest and western continuation
periods.summary: Northern Wei conquered the Gansu kingdom; Juqu relatives continued farther west before Rouran conquest in 460.

items.text: In 397, Juqu Mengxun’s rebellion helped place Duan Ye on the throne. Mengxun later removed him and became ruler himself. By 412 he held Guzang, near modern Wuwei. Northern Liang’s beginning was therefore a sequence of shifting alliances and rulers, rather than one peaceful founding ceremony.

Hexi offered a comparatively sheltered destination for people escaping warfare farther east. Scholars carried books and learning with them, while Buddhist monks traveled through the corridor. Northern Liang’s cultural influence grew partly from welcoming skills and traditions already developed elsewhere.

Political loyalties can hide inside a date. Northern Liang artifacts sometimes use the reign names of the neighboring Xia or Northern Wei rulers. A clothing inventory dated 436 uses a form of the Northern Wei era name. These small written choices help historians trace the kingdom’s efforts to accommodate stronger powers.

In contemporary Turfan, farther west than the map’s Gansu outline, silk production grew as migrants arrived through Hexi. Northern Liang-period tax records calculate silk obligations using land holdings and household population. Family size could therefore matter to an official as well as to whoever was counting bowls at dinner.

A fragment from Kara-Khoja Tomb 91 in the Turfan region records wheat owed as land rent during the first half of the fifth century. It connects fields, a staple food and official accounting. Grain was useful enough to be collected directly; these fragments preserve part of the farming economy behind long-distance trade.

A small stupa from Jiuquan, dated 434, records Bai Shuangju’s hope that relatives and ancestors from seven generations would eventually encounter Maitreya, the future Buddha. This was a religious wish, not a report of something observed. Family remembrance could reach much farther back than grandparents.

The donor of a different Jiuquan stupa, dated 429, remembered parents and a ruler together. Such dedications made personal family obligations visible in religious objects. A stone monument could preserve the concerns of a named patron whose ordinary conversations have vanished.

sections.title: Making art and learning in caves

items.text: Bai Shuangju’s 434 stupa survives in three stacked portions: an eight-sided base, a cylindrical body and a rounded shoulder. A projecting tenon underneath shows that it once fitted into another support. Even a sacred monument needed a practical way to hold its pieces together.

The same stupa combines carved scripture with Buddha and bodhisattva figures. The museum explains the images as linking past, present and future, including Maitreya. Text and sculpture worked together to express Buddhist teachings, so the decoration carried meaning beyond making the stone look impressive.

Dunhuang’s cliff rock contains loose sand and pebbles, making it unsuitable for elaborate stone carving. Artists instead made painted clay figures and murals. The landscape helped shape the technique: a cliff full of Buddhist images did not mean that every image was carved from the cliff itself.

Mogao Cave 268 belongs to an early design with a main chamber and tiny adjoining meditation cells. The Dunhuang Academy describes these cells as just large enough for a person to practice inside. This was a setting for concentrated religious training, with very little room for pacing about.

Researchers dated plant material from the clay cores of statues and from wall plaster in three early Mogao caves. Straw, reeds and chaff can preserve a construction clue long after their builders are forgotten. Materials hidden inside an artwork can be as informative as the painted surface.

A 2018 study combined radiocarbon results with archaeological evidence and a statistical model, placing the early construction of Caves 268 and 272, together with Cave 275, around 410 to 440. This supports a fifth-century setting while leaving room for uncertainty and alterations. The result is a date range, not an inscription naming a single opening day.

A surviving Sixteen Kingdoms manuscript fragment copies letters by Pan Yue, an earlier writer. Displayed by the Gansu museum, it illustrates the broader Five Liang region’s interest in literature. Copying a respected author kept both his words and the work of handwriting alive during political upheaval.

sections.title: A written voice and a changing world

items.text: The 429 Jiuquan stupa includes the Chinese phrase “為父母君王”, meaning “for parents and the ruler”. These characters are shown in modern scholarly transcription of the inscription, not as a facsimile of its carved handwriting. A short phrase carries a very human list of people the donor wanted to honor.

Northern Wei’s conquest in 439 uprooted Northern Liang communities. People were forcibly resettled around Pingcheng, modern Datong. Juqu relatives escaped westward and continued resisting from Gaochang, where they controlled important routes. Military victory changed where people lived and worked, as well as who collected their allegiance.

Craft workers moved to Pingcheng after the conquest and helped make Buddhist temples and images there. Northern Liang’s government had lost power, but its artistic skills traveled with people. The small stupas and caves of Hexi belong to a history that continued beyond the kingdom’s borders and lifetime.

ending.text: Northern Wei conquered Northern Liang’s Gansu kingdom in 439. The Juqu family’s western continuation around Gaochang survived until Rouran conquest in 460. Neither event ended the region’s communities or Buddhist artistic traditions. The atlas’s 500 endpoint is a coarse map cutoff, not a further Northern Liang reign.
